core: Continuity and change as a historical-thinking lens: examining what stayed the same alongside what shifted over time
Continuity can be as historically significant as change; beginners tend to overweight dramatic change
Change and continuity occur simultaneously, and different aspects of life change at different paces
Periodization: dividing the past into named blocks of time to make study possible
Periods are interpretive constructs with fuzzy, debated boundaries and culturally specific (often Western-centric) labels
Turning points, and the distinction between gradual/evolutionary and rapid/revolutionary change

claims.claim: Continuity and change is one of the core historical-thinking concepts; it asks historians to consider not only change but also continuity, because the absence of upheaval and the maintenance of continuity can be as historically significant as change.
Change and continuity occur at the same time; change happens at different paces at different times, and even at the same time in different aspects of life.

Periodization is the process of categorizing the past into named blocks of time in order to facilitate study and analysis; period names take varied forms, such as events (the inter-war years, 1918-1939), decades (the 1960s), individuals (the Victorian Era), and cultural nicknames (the Gilded Age).

Systems of periodization are constructs: determining the precise beginning and ending of any period involves arbitrary, interpretive decisions, and periodizing labels reflect particular cultural and geographic (often Western) perspectives that fit non-Western histories poorly.

The Western Roman Empire is traditionally said to have ended on 4 September 476 CE, when Odoacer deposed the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, and made himself king of Italy; this date is a conventional marker often used to separate antiquity from the Middle Ages, and the empire had already been in decline for decades, so the change was gradual.

The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire continued long after the Western Empire fell, existing until 1453 CE, so the 476 turning point coincides with major continuity; moreover, historians dispute when the 'Byzantine' period itself begins, dating it variously to 330, 476, 565, or around 650 CE.

conflictingEvidence.issue: When the 'Byzantine' or medieval period actually begins, and whether 476 CE is a meaningful break.
positions: The deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE is the traditional marker for the end of the Western Roman Empire and the start of the Middle Ages.

Many historians emphasize continuity across this transition and place the boundary of the Byzantine/medieval era elsewhere (e.g., 330, 565, or c. 650 CE), or prefer a 'Late Antiquity' framing that de-emphasizes any single break.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 476 CE only as a conventional marker and explicitly presents the disagreement over the boundary as an illustration of the topic's core point, that periods are interpretive constructs with fuzzy boundaries. It does not assert that 476 was the moment 'everything changed.'

sourceRecords.notes: Describes the six historical-thinking concepts developed by Peter Seixas and the Historical Thinking Project, one of which is 'continuity and change.' Supports: continuity as well as change must be considered; the absence of upheaval and maintenance of continuity can be historically significant; change happens at different paces and even at the same time in different aspects of life; and the concept's link to periodization and turning points. sourceRecords.title: Splitting History (Periodization) — World History (Boundless)
sourceRecords.notes: Open CC BY world-history survey (Boundless). Supports: periodization is categorizing the past into named blocks of time to facilitate study; all systems of periodization are arbitrary and the precise start/end of a period is an arbitrary decision; period labels reflect particular cultural and geographic (Western) perspectives and fit Asian or African histories poorly; and examples of period-name types (Gilded Age; inter-war years 1918-1939; the 1960s; Victorian Era). Facts synthesized; all prose original, no source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Last Roman Emperor Is Deposed (Research Starter)
sourceRecords.notes: Reference article. Supports the dated example: on 4 September 476 CE Romulus Augustulus was overthrown by Odoacer, who declared himself king of Italy; the end of the Roman part of the empire is traditionally said to have occurred in 476; and the empire had been in decline for decades due to internal strife and Germanic invasions, so the fall was gradual. Used REFERENCE_ONLY for verified dates and framing only.

sourceRecords.title: Byzantine Empire
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry. Supports: the Byzantine (Eastern Roman) Empire existed from 330 to 1453 CE, continuing long after the Western Empire fell; and that scholars disagree about when the 'Byzantine' period begins, variously selecting 330, the Western fall in 476, the failure of Justinian I in 565, or c. 650 CE, which directly illustrates the fuzzy-boundary point about periodization.
